title: Episode 2: Understanding GitHub on the Web
description: How GitHub organizes its web pages, heading structure, landmarks, and keyboard shortcuts.
concepts: GitHub page types: dashboard, repository, issue, pull request, profile, settings
The HTML heading hierarchy GitHub uses on each page type
ARIA landmarks and regions on GitHub pages
The global navigation bar and how to reach it by keyboard
GitHub built-in keyboard shortcuts: pressing ? to see them
The jump-to-content skip link on every GitHub page
How to orient yourself on an unfamiliar page using headings
The command palette: / or Control+K for quick navigation
The difference between GitHub.com and github.dev
transcriptText:
﻿[ALEX]
Welcome back. Before we do deeper GitHub work, we need a mental map. If GitHub has ever felt like a maze of tabs, sidebars, and pages that all blur together, this lesson is here to fix that.

[JAMIE]
And this is especially important for learners using screen readers, magnification, zoom, high contrast themes, or just anyone who wants a reliable way to know, where am I, and what kind of page is this?

[ALEX]
Exactly. And one quick administrative note before we begin: this lesson pairs with an audio episode and with two appendices, a glossary and a screen reader cheat sheet. It also points learners to GitHub's own docs and GitHub accessibility documentation as the authoritative references.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just theory. It's the orientation system for everything that comes next.

[ALEX]
Yes. Read or listen to this before navigating GitHub for the first time, because once you understand page structure, landmarks, headings, and URL patterns, you can orient yourself on pages this course never explicitly teaches.

[JAMIE]
And there was also a course-planning note here, right?

[ALEX]
Right. The chapter connects directly to a challenge called Find Your Way Around, which uses ideas from this lesson plus the next repository navigation lessons. And there's a capstone connection too: when you later build AI agents, those agents work through GitHub objects like issues, pull requests, and labels. So learning the manual workflow now is also learning how to collaborate with automation later.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's start with the big picture. GitHub is not one page. It's three nested levels.

[JAMIE]
I love that already, because many beginners think GitHub is just, quote, the repo page.

[ALEX]
Yes, but the repo is only one level. Level one is your own account area: your profile, settings, notifications. Think URLs like github dot com slash your username, or slash settings, or slash notifications.

[JAMIE]
So that's personal space.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Level two is an organization or another user's space. That might be github dot com slash microsoft, or slash community-access, or slash github. That's the public home area for a person or organization.

[JAMIE]
And level three is the repository.

[ALEX]
The place where most actual project work happens. Code, issues, pull requests, actions, discussions around changes. A URL like github dot com slash owner slash repo. Or that same path plus slash issues, or slash pull slash 42.

[JAMIE]
So when someone says, go to the repo, they mean level three.

[ALEX]
Almost always. And here's a very useful orientation tip for screen reader users: jump to the first level-one heading. On a repository page, the H1 is usually owner slash repo name. On a profile page, it's the username. On a settings page, it's the settings category. The first heading tells you the level.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's talk about what stays consistent, because that's calming.

[ALEX]
Yes. No matter where you are on GitHub, there is a global navigation bar at the top. It is your fixed anchor point.

[JAMIE]
Even if the visual layout shifts around?

[ALEX]
Yes, and that's an important teaching principle in this chapter: don't over-trust position words like top-right, left side, first, below. GitHub changes layout density, feature rollout, and wrapping over time, and the page can look different depending on screen width or account state.

[JAMIE]
So instead of saying, click the thing in the top-right, we should anchor to stable identifiers.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Use URL pattern, page title, H1 heading, landmark name, tab name, keyboard shortcut, command name, or exact button text. Those are much more dependable.

[JAMIE]
What's in the global navigation area?

[ALEX]
Commonly: the GitHub logo or home link, global search, a Copilot entry point, links to pull requests and issues across GitHub, notifications, and the profile avatar menu.

[JAMIE]
And for a screen reader user, the key point is not just what the controls are, but where they live.

[ALEX]
Right. They live in the landmark labeled Navigation Menu. If you press D to cycle landmarks, you'll hear Navigation Menu. Once you're there, K moves through links inside that landmark.

[JAMIE]
And those links are just regular links, not special controls that require forms mode or focus mode.

[ALEX]
Correct. That's explicitly called out. In browse mode, press Enter on the links and they work.

[JAMIE]
Can we give the shortcut highlights too?

[ALEX]
Definitely. Search is often reachable with S or slash. Notifications can be reached with G then N. And if you're moving by landmarks and links, D to Navigation Menu, then K through the available links is a reliable pattern.

[JAMIE]
What changes once you're inside a repository?

[ALEX]
You get a second navigation bar below the global one: repository navigation. That's where tabs like Code, Issues, Pull requests, Actions, Projects, Wiki, Security, Insights, and Settings appear.

[JAMIE]
And that landmark has a name too.

[ALEX]
Yes: Repository navigation. So on repo pages, you often have two crucial navigation landmarks to recognize: Navigation Menu for GitHub-wide controls, and Repository navigation for this specific project.

[JAMIE]
The learning cards in this section also addressed different users.

[ALEX]
They did. For screen reader users: Navigation Menu is the fixed anchor on every page, G then N jumps to notifications, and search results load into Main after using search. For low vision users: the top navigation stays pinned, the notification bell may show an unread dot or badge, and repository tabs show the active tab with a colored underline, which may be easier to perceive in a high contrast theme. For sighted users: remember the visual pattern of a global top bar and then repository tabs below it.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay, if I'm dropped onto some random GitHub page, how do I tell where I am without guessing?

[ALEX]
Use three signals: the URL, the browser tab title, and the first H1 heading.

[JAMIE]
Let's do the URL first.

[ALEX]
GitHub URLs are wonderfully descriptive. Plain github dot com is your home or personal feed. Github dot com slash username is a user profile. Github dot com slash org is an organization profile. Github dot com slash owner slash repo is the repository home, usually the Code tab.

[JAMIE]
And then adding path pieces tells the story.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Slash issues means the issues list. Slash issues slash 42 means issue number 42. Slash pull slash 7 means pull request 7. Slash tree slash main slash docs means a folder view. Slash blob slash main slash README dot md means a file view. Slash commit slash some hash means a commit page. Slash settings slash accessibility is your accessibility settings. Slash notifications is your notifications inbox.

[JAMIE]
And if someone uses a screen reader and wants to verify that quickly?

[ALEX]
Go to the browser address bar. Alt+D on Windows or Command+L on Mac. Listen to the URL. That alone often tells you where you are.

[JAMIE]
Second signal: browser tab title.

[ALEX]
GitHub titles are also patterned. Repository home might be owner slash repo, then a short description, then GitHub. Issues list is Issues dot owner slash repo. A specific issue includes the issue title, then Issue number, then owner slash repo. A pull request includes the PR title, then Pull Request number, then owner slash repo. Notifications says Notifications dash GitHub. Settings pages often say category dash Settings.

[JAMIE]
And the third signal is the first H1.

[ALEX]
Yes. In browse mode, press 1 to jump to the first H1. If you hear owner slash repo, you're on repository home. If you hear Issues, you're on the issues list. If you hear an issue title, you're on an issue detail page. If you hear a PR title, you're on a pull request page. If you hear your username, you're on your profile. If you hear a settings category, you're in settings.

[JAMIE]
That is a very teachable routine: URL, title, H1.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Three independent signals. If all three agree, you can trust your orientation.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now we get into the page types people actually use all the time.

[ALEX]
Yes. The lesson identifies five key page types. If you can recognize these, GitHub becomes much less mysterious.

[JAMIE]
Page type one: repository home on the Code tab.

[ALEX]
This is the central hub of a project. Expect the H1 to be owner slash repo-name. Expect the Repository navigation tabs. Expect a file tree, usually presented as a table. Screen reader users may navigate to the next table and then use table navigation commands such as Control+Alt with arrow keys, depending on screen reader and browser. Below the file tree, you'll often find the rendered README.

[JAMIE]
And usually some sidebar information too.

[ALEX]
Right. Commonly an About panel, metadata, release or package info, and project-related side content. The exact arrangement can vary by viewport, but the concepts stay the same: project identity, tabs, file list, README, related metadata.

[JAMIE]
Page type two is the issues list.

[ALEX]
The issues list is not one issue. It's the catalog of issues for a repository. Expect the H1 to be Issues. Expect filters and search controls. Expect a list or table-like collection of issue rows, often showing issue title, issue number, labels, author, and update metadata.

[JAMIE]
So this page answers, what open or closed issues exist in this repo?

[ALEX]
Exactly. It's the scanning page.

[JAMIE]
Page type three is issue detail.

[ALEX]
Now you're inside one specific issue. The H1 is the issue title. Nearby you'll usually find the issue number and state, such as open or closed. The main content area typically contains the original issue description and a threaded timeline of comments and events.

[JAMIE]
And then a sidebar with metadata.

[ALEX]
Yes. Things like assignees, labels, projects, milestones, participants, or linked development information. The key idea is that issue detail is a conversation page around one tracked piece of work.

[JAMIE]
Page type four is pull request detail.

[ALEX]
Another conversation page, but specifically about proposed code changes. The H1 is the pull request title. You'll encounter tabs like Conversation, Commits, Checks, and Files changed. The Conversation tab looks somewhat like an issue thread, but it includes review events, approval states, requested changes, CI checks, merge status, and code-related discussion.

[JAMIE]
And the Files Changed tab is a distinct mode.

[ALEX]
Very much so. That's where you inspect diffs. It has its own structure and is often denser, especially for screen reader users.

[JAMIE]
Then page type five combines your personal feed and your profile.

[ALEX]
Right. Your feed, at github dot com, is your activity hub: updates from repositories and people you follow, recent work, notifications of interest, suggested activity. Your profile, at github dot com slash your username, is your identity page: your name or username, bio, pinned repositories, contribution activity, repositories tab, and public-facing account information.

[JAMIE]
So feed is what is happening around you, and profile is who you are on GitHub.

[ALEX]
That's a nice concise distinction.

[JAMIE]
Were there learning card takeaways for this whole section?

[ALEX]
Yes: train yourself to classify a page quickly. Is it a repo home, issues list, issue detail, PR detail, feed, or profile? Once you know the type, you can predict landmarks, headings, controls, and what task is possible there.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's build a more concrete mental image of a repository page.

[ALEX]
Picture a repository home page as layers. First, the global Navigation Menu at the top. Then the Repository navigation bar with tabs like Code and Issues. Then the main content area with repository identity and controls. After that, the file tree listing folders and files. Then the rendered README below. And often alongside or after the main stream, a sidebar with About and other metadata.

[JAMIE]
So for a sighted learner, this is a visual stack. For a screen reader user, it becomes a landmark and heading sequence.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And the lesson explicitly includes screen reader navigation of this type of page. A practical pattern is: jump by landmarks first, confirm the H1, move to Repository navigation if you need tabs, move into Main, then use headings, tables, and links to inspect the file list and README.

[JAMIE]
So don't just arrow from the top of the page and hope.

[ALEX]
Right. Use structure intentionally.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
That leads perfectly into the screen reader orientation sequence.

[ALEX]
Yes. This is one of the most important practical parts of the lesson. When you land on a GitHub page, use a consistent sequence.

[JAMIE]
Walk us through it.

[ALEX]
Step one: identify the page using URL, tab title, or H1. Step two: jump through landmarks with D so you know the major regions available. Step three: listen for Navigation Menu and, if you're inside a repository, Repository navigation. Step four: jump to the H1 with 1 and confirm the page type. Step five: move into Main and use headings, links, buttons, tables, and lists based on the page's purpose.

[JAMIE]
So instead of, where do I start, you always start with the same ritual.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That's the point of the learning cards here: orientation should become procedural. Land on page. Check URL. Check title. Check H1. Scan landmarks. Then act.

[JAMIE]
That kind of repeatable routine lowers cognitive load.

[ALEX]
A lot.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's get even more specific: landmark structure by page type.

[ALEX]
Right. Different GitHub pages share some landmarks, but each page type tends to have a recognizable pattern.

[JAMIE]
Start with repository home.

[ALEX]
Repository home often includes the Navigation Menu landmark first, then Repository navigation, then Main. Within Main, you may encounter search or filtering controls, a table for the file tree, regions related to README content, and complementary or aside-style information depending on browser and accessibility tree exposure.

[JAMIE]
Issues list page?

[ALEX]
Again, Navigation Menu, then Repository navigation, then Main. Inside Main, expect filtering controls, issue list content, and possibly pagination or additional controls.

[JAMIE]
Issue detail?

[ALEX]
Navigation Menu, Repository navigation, Main. But Main now contains a page heading for the issue title, the issue metadata, the conversation timeline, comment composer, and sidebar metadata such as labels or assignees.

[JAMIE]
Pull request conversation tab?

[ALEX]
Similar to issue detail in landmark flow, but Main includes pull request status information, branch and merge context, review conversation, checks, and related controls.

[JAMIE]
And Files Changed?

[ALEX]
Still under the same broader shell, but Main becomes diff-centric. Expect file-by-file changed sections, controls for viewing or filtering diffs, and a much more granular navigation experience. This is where headings and quick navigation between file sections become especially helpful.

[JAMIE]
So the lesson isn't promising that landmarks are identical forever, but it is teaching a durable expectation pattern.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The stable lesson is the order of orientation: global shell, repo shell if applicable, then page-specific main content.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's pair that with heading hierarchy, because landmarks get you to regions, but headings tell you the internal outline.

[ALEX]
Well said. On repository home, the H1 is owner slash repo. Lower-level headings may introduce content sections like README areas, releases, or side panels, depending on page structure.

[JAMIE]
On the issues list, the H1 is simply Issues.

[ALEX]
Yes, and subheadings may group content or support filtering and list organization.

[JAMIE]
On issue detail, the H1 is the issue title.

[ALEX]
Then lower headings can identify conversation blocks, side sections, or related metadata areas.

[JAMIE]
For pull request detail on the Conversation tab, the H1 is the PR title.

[ALEX]
And below that, headings may separate status, timeline content, reviews, checks summaries, and related sections.

[JAMIE]
While on Files Changed, the heading structure often helps you hop between changed files.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Files Changed tends to reward heading navigation because each file section can act like a chunk you want to inspect independently.

[JAMIE]
So the learning card takeaway is to not just use heading navigation randomly. Use it with a prediction based on page type.

[ALEX]
Yes. Know what H1 should be, then use the rest of the heading tree as your internal map of the page.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's talk about viewport, because GitHub can feel like a moving target when you zoom or shrink the browser.

[ALEX]
And that's normal. At full desktop width, roughly twelve hundred pixels and up, GitHub often presents side-by-side layouts. Sidebars are more likely to stay alongside main content. Navigation elements may all appear expanded.

[JAMIE]
At tablet widths?

[ALEX]
Roughly seven hundred sixty-eight to just under twelve hundred pixels, elements may wrap. Sidebars may shift lower. Controls may compress. The same information is still present, but not necessarily in the same visual arrangement.

[JAMIE]
And on mobile widths below that?

[ALEX]
Layouts become more stacked and condensed. Menus may collapse. Side content often moves below main content. Some control labels may shorten or become icon-triggered. This matters for both mobile devices and desktop users who zoom heavily.

[JAMIE]
So again, don't anchor too strongly to spatial instructions.

[ALEX]
Exactly. This is why the chapter insists on durable cues: names, landmarks, headings, URLs, buttons, tabs, and shortcuts. Those survive viewport shifts better than screen position descriptions.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now for the mental model itself. If you wanted a learner to carry one internal picture away from this lesson, what is it?

[ALEX]
I would say this: every GitHub page is a shell plus a page type. The shell is the global navigation, and sometimes repository navigation. The page type is the specific work surface: repo home, issues list, issue detail, PR detail, profile, feed, and so on.

[JAMIE]
So first identify the shell, then identify the page type.

[ALEX]
Yes. Then predict what should be there. On repo home, expect files and README. On issues list, expect filters and issue rows. On issue detail, expect a conversation thread plus metadata. On PR detail, expect review and changed files. On feed, expect activity. On profile, identity and repositories.

[JAMIE]
That predictive ability is what makes a site stop feeling random.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The learning cards call this building your internal map. You're not memorizing every page. You're learning how to infer structure from a few reliable signals.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The lesson also includes a practice activity: the 60-second orientation.

[ALEX]
Yes. Here's the exercise. Open any GitHub page and give yourself one minute. First, identify the URL pattern. Second, listen to or inspect the browser tab title. Third, jump to the H1. Fourth, cycle landmarks. Fifth, state out loud what page type you're on and what you expect to find next.

[JAMIE]
That's a great habit.

[ALEX]
It is. You can do it on a repository home, an issues list, an issue detail page, a pull request, your notifications, or your profile. The goal is not speed for its own sake. The goal is certainty.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And if someone gets stuck?

[ALEX]
Return to the three signals. Check the URL. Check the tab title. Check the first H1. Then jump by landmarks. If needed, go back to a simpler known page like the repository Code tab or your notifications page. Use the glossary. Use the screen reader cheat sheet. And when GitHub's layout feels different than expected, trust labels and landmark names more than visual position.

[JAMIE]
That's such an important accessibility reminder: the page may have changed shape, but it usually hasn't changed identity.

[ALEX]
Beautifully put.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There was also a short Day 2 amplifier in the chapter.

[ALEX]
Yes. The idea is that this orientation skill becomes even more powerful the next day when you start working with automation and AI agents. Agents operate through the same objects you now understand: issues, pull requests, labels, repository pages. So a solid mental model of GitHub's structure is foundational, not optional.

[JAMIE]
Before we close, can you give a compact recap?

[ALEX]
Sure. GitHub has three levels: personal account, organization or user space, and repository. Every page has a global Navigation Menu. Repository pages also have Repository navigation. You can orient using URL, browser tab title, and the first H1. Learn the five key page types: repository home, issues list, issue detail, pull request detail, and your feed or profile. Use landmarks first, then headings. Expect layouts to change across desktop, tablet, mobile, and high zoom. Build an internal map so you can predict what belongs on each page.

[JAMIE]
And if you're using a screen reader, make your routine automatic: address bar if needed, 1 for H1, D for landmarks, K for links within navigation, and stable labels over visual guesswork.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Once you stop treating GitHub as a giant undifferentiated website and start recognizing its page types and structure, it becomes teachable, navigable, and much less stressful.

[JAMIE]
That's the goal. We'll build on that from here.

# Understanding GitHub's Web Structure
>
> **Listen to Episode 2:** [Understanding GitHub on the Web](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md) | [Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/start-your-journey/about-github-and-git) | [GitHub Accessibility Documentation](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation)

## How GitHub Is Organized, and How to Orient Yourself on Every Page

> **Read this before navigating GitHub for the first time.** This lesson gives you the mental model that makes every subsequent guide easier. Once you understand how GitHub pages are built - their landmark structure, heading hierarchy, and URL patterns - you will know how to orient yourself on any page you land on, even ones this guide never mentions.

## Table of Contents

> **Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around** uses the concepts from this chapter and [Chapter 03](03-navigating-repositories.md) and [Chapter 04](04-the-learning-room.md). Read this chapter first to build the mental model, then navigate repositories with confidence.

1. [GitHub's Three-Level Structure](#1-githubs-three-level-structure)
2. [What Is Always on Every GitHub Page](#2-what-is-always-on-every-github-page)
3. [How to Tell Where You Are](#3-how-to-tell-where-you-are)
4. [The Five Key Page Types](#4-the-five-key-page-types)
5. [Visual Map of a Repository Page](#5-visual-map-of-a-repository-page)
6. [Screen Reader Orientation Sequence](#6-screen-reader-orientation-sequence)
7. [Landmark Structure by Page Type](#7-landmark-structure-by-page-type)
8. [GitHub's Heading Hierarchy in Practice](#8-githubs-heading-hierarchy-in-practice)
9. [How GitHub's Layout Changes by Viewport](#9-how-githubs-layout-changes-by-viewport)
10. [The Mental Model - Building Your Internal Map](#10-the-mental-model---building-your-internal-map)

> **The Capstone Connection:** By the end of tomorrow, you will build your own customized AI Agent. But agents do not have magic portals into your code — they read Issues, they write Pull Requests, and they trigger on Labels. Think of GitHub as the operating system for AI. As you learn these manual features today, you are actually learning how to converse with the agents you will build tomorrow.

## 1. GitHub's Three-Level Structure

GitHub is not a single page or a single kind of page. It is three nested levels, and understanding which level you are on changes how you navigate.

```text
    Level 1: Your Account / Profile
   github.com/your-username
   github.com/settings/...
   github.com/notifications

Level 2: An Organization or User's Space
   github.com/microsoft
   github.com/community-access
   github.com/github

Level 3: A Repository - where all the work happens
   github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents
   github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents/issues
   github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents/pull/42
```

**Most of this workshop happens at Level 3.** Issues, pull requests, code, and actions all live inside a repository. When someone says "go to the repo," they mean Level 3.

> **Screen reader orientation tip:** The first heading (`H` then `1`) on any page tells you what level you are on. On a repository page, it reads "owner/repo-name." On your profile page, it reads your username. On a settings page, it reads the settings category name.

## 2. What Is Always on Every GitHub Page

No matter where you navigate on GitHub, the same global navigation bar is at the top of every page. Understanding its landmark structure means you always have a fixed orientation point.

> **Dependable walkthrough principle:** GitHub changes visual placement, density, wrapping, and feature rollout over time. Treat position words such as "top-right," "left side," "first," and "below" as orientation hints only. For reliable teaching, anchor each step on the stable thing a learner can verify: URL pattern, page title, H1 heading, landmark name, tab name, keyboard shortcut, command name, or button text.

### The Global Navigation Bar (always present)

Visually, the top bar commonly contains the following controls. The order and compactness can change with viewport width, account state, and product rollout:

| Element | What It Is | How to Reach It |
| ---  | ---  | ---  |
| GitHub logo / home link | Returns to your personal feed | First link in "Navigation Menu" landmark |
| Search bar | Global search across all of GitHub | `S` or `/` shortcut; or `D` → Navigation Menu → `K` to search |
| Copilot icon | Quick access to GitHub Copilot chat | `K` navigation from search bar |
| Pull Requests | Your PRs across all repos | `K` navigation |
| Issues | Your issues across all repos | `K` navigation |
| Notifications (bell) | Your notification inbox | `G` then `N` shortcut |
| Profile avatar | Account menu, settings, sign out | `K` to last link in nav; or go directly via URL |

**Screen reader landmark:** All of these live inside the landmark labeled **"Navigation Menu"**. Press `D` to cycle landmarks until you hear "Navigation Menu," then press `K` to move through the links inside it.

> **Important:** These are standard anchor links. You do not need to switch to Focus Mode to activate them. Press `Enter` in Browse Mode and they work.

### Secondary navigation (repository pages only)

When you are inside a repository, a second navigation bar appears below the global bar. This contains the repository's tabs: Code, Issues, Pull requests, Actions, Projects, Wiki, Security, Insights, and Settings.

**Screen reader landmark:** This is labeled **"Repository navigation"**. Press `D` to jump to it directly.

### Learning Cards: What Is Always on Every GitHub Page

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Press `D` to cycle landmarks; the first landmark on every page is "Navigation Menu" -- this is your fixed anchor point
- Press `G` then `N` (two keystrokes in sequence) to jump directly to Notifications from any GitHub page
- The global search field is reachable with `S` or `/`; after searching, results load into the Main landmark -- press `D` to jump there

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- The global navigation bar is pinned to the top of every page; at 200%+ zoom it may shrink icons but keeps all items in a single row
- The notification bell shows an unread count as a blue dot (or a number badge); zoom in on the top-right corner to see it clearly
- Repository tabs below the global bar highlight the active tab with a colored underline; switch to a high-contrast theme if the underline is hard to see

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The global nav bar runs across the top: GitHub logo (left), search bar (center), and profile avatar/bell icon (right)
- Inside a repository, a second row of tabs (Code, Issues, Pull requests, etc.) appears below the global bar; the active tab has a bold underline
- The notification bell icon in the top-right shows a blue dot when you have unread notifications

</details>

## 3. How to Tell Where You Are

Three signals tell you exactly where you are on GitHub, without needing to see the visual layout:

### Signal 1: The URL

GitHub URLs are readable descriptions of your location:

| URL pattern | Where you are |
| ---  | ---  |
| `github.com` | Your personal feed / home |
| `github.com/username` | A user profile page |
| `github.com/org` | An organization profile |
| `github.com/owner/repo` | Repository home page (Code tab) |
| `github.com/owner/repo/issues` | Issues list |
| `github.com/owner/repo/issues/42` | A specific issue (number 42) |
| `github.com/owner/repo/pull/7` | A specific pull request (number 7) |
| `github.com/owner/repo/tree/main/docs` | A folder inside the repo |
| `github.com/owner/repo/blob/main/README.md` | A specific file |
| `github.com/owner/repo/commit/a1b2c3d` | A specific commit |
| `github.com/settings/accessibility` | Your accessibility settings |
| `github.com/notifications` | Your notification inbox |

**Screen reader tip:** Your browser's address bar is always reachable with `Alt+D` (Windows) or `Cmd+L` (Mac). Press it, listen to the URL, and you will know exactly where you are.

### Signal 2: The browser tab title

GitHub formats page titles consistently:

| Page type | Title format |
| ---  | ---  |
| Repository home | `owner/repo: Short description - GitHub` |
| Issues list | `Issues · owner/repo` |
| Specific issue | `Issue title · Issue #42 · owner/repo` |
| Pull request | `PR title · Pull Request #7 · owner/repo` |
| Your notifications | `Notifications - GitHub` |
| Settings | `Category - Settings` |

### Signal 3: The first H1 heading

Press `1` (in Browse Mode) on any GitHub page to jump to the first H1 heading. What you hear tells you what type of page you are on:

| You hear | You are on |
| ---  | ---  |
| `owner/repo-name` | Repository home page |
| `Issues` | Issues list |
| The issue title | Issue detail page |
| The PR title | Pull request detail page |
| Your username | Your profile page |
| A settings category name | A settings page |

## 4. The Five Key Page Types

### Page Type 1: Repository Home (Code Tab)

This is the central hub of any project. It is where you find the file tree, the README, branch information, and links to all other parts of the repository.

#### What to expect

- H1: `owner/repo-name`
- Repository navigation landmark (Code, Issues, PRs, Actions tabs)
- A file tree table - navigate with `T` then `Ctrl+Alt+Arrow`
- A rendered README below the file tree
- A sidebar with About, Topics, Releases, Contributors

### Page Type 2: Issues List

A searchable, filterable list of all issues in the repository.

#### What to expect

- H1: `Issues`
- A search and filter bar at the top
- Each issue is a link with: issue title, labels, number, author, comment count
- Issue titles are H3 headings - press `3` to jump between them
- Landmark: "Search Results List"

### Page Type 3: Issue Detail

The full view of a single issue: the original report, all comments, labels, assignees, and the timeline.

#### What to expect

- H1: The issue title
- H2: "Description" (original issue body)
- H2: "Activity" (comments and events)
- Landmark: "Add a comment" (the reply box at the bottom)
- Sidebar: assignees, labels, milestone, linked PRs

### Page Type 4: Pull Request Detail

The most complex page on GitHub - it has three tabs (Conversation, Commits, Files Changed), each with its own structure.

#### What to expect

- H1: The PR title
- Landmark: "Pull request tabs" (Conversation, Commits, Files changed)
- Conversation tab: same structure as an issue detail
- Files Changed tab: a file tree on the left + diff view on the right
- Landmark: "Pull request navigation tabs" - use `D` to reach it, then `Left`/`Right Arrow` to switch tabs

### Page Type 5: Your Personal Feed and Profile

Your personal home (`github.com`) shows activity from repositories you follow. Your profile (`github.com/username`) shows your contribution graph, pinned repos, and bio.

#### What to expect on your feed

- A "For you" activity stream - recent activity from repos you watch
- A sidebar of suggested repositories and topics

#### What to expect on your profile

- H1: Your username
- A contribution activity graph (visually prominent; read as a table by screen readers)
- Pinned repositories
- A list of your recent public activity

- On an Issue Detail page, press `3` to jump between H3 comment headers; each announces the author and timestamp
- On the PR Files Changed tab, press `3` to jump between file name headings; press `4` to jump between diff hunk headers inside each file

</details>

- Issue labels appear as small colored badges next to each title in the Issues list; zoom to 150%+ so the label text is readable
- On the PR Files Changed tab, additions are shaded green and deletions are shaded red; high-contrast themes use bolder shading

</details>

<details>

- The Issues list shows a green "Open" or red "Closed" icon next to each issue title, plus label badges and comment count icons
- Pull request tabs (Conversation, Commits, Files changed) appear as a horizontal bar just below the PR title

## 5. Visual Map of a Repository Page

> **See also:** [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md) defines every term used in this course. [Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md) has quick-reference keyboard shortcuts for navigating headings and landmarks.

### Description

A repository home page is laid out from top to bottom as follows. The Global Navigation bar (landmark: "Navigation Menu") contains the GitHub logo, Search, Copilot, Pull Requests, Issues, Notifications bell, and your avatar. Below that are the Repository Tabs (landmark: "Repository navigation") showing Code, Issues (12), Pull requests (3), Actions, and more. Next is the Repository Header, which is the H1 heading "owner / repo-name" plus Star (42), Watch, and Fork (8) buttons. The main content area is split into two columns. On the left is the File Area with the branch selector (main), Go to file button, Code button, and the File Table (a landmark) listing files like .github/, docs/, and README.md with dates. On the right is the Sidebar with the About section, description text, topics (accessibility), Releases (3), Contributors (5), and Languages (Markdown 100%). Below both columns is the rendered README (landmark: "Repository files navigation"), and at the bottom is the Footer.

### Screen reader navigation of this page

Press 1 to hear "owner/repo-name" (the H1, confirms you are on the right repo). Press D to hear "Navigation Menu," then D again for "Repository navigation," then D again for "Main" (the file tree area). Press T to jump to the file table, then Ctrl+Alt+Down Arrow to navigate rows. Press D again to reach "Repository files navigation" and read the README.

## 6. Screen Reader Orientation Sequence

Do this every time you land on a new GitHub page. It takes about 10 seconds once you are practiced. Make it automatic.

<details>
<summary>Visual / mouse users - page orientation</summary>

When you land on a GitHub page, scan these areas to orient yourself:

1. **Browser tab title** - tells you the page type and repo context
2. **Global nav bar** (top strip) - GitHub logo, search box, bells/icons
3. **Repo tabs** (below global nav, visible only inside a repo) - Code, Issues, Pull Requests, etc.
4. **H1 heading** - tells you exactly what page you're on (repo name / "Issues" / issue title / PR title)
5. **Main content area** - file tree, issue list, PR diff, etc.

That's your visual map. Click anything visible to navigate.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (NVDA / JAWS) - 10-second orientation sequence</summary>

```text
Step 1: Press 1
        → Hear: what page type are you on? (repo name / "Issues" / issue title / PR title)

Step 2: Press D repeatedly
        → Hear: what landmark regions exist on this page?
        → Build a map: "Navigation Menu, Repository navigation, Main, Add a comment, Pagination"

Step 3: Press NVDA+F7 (NVDA) or Insert+F3 (JAWS)
        → Open the Elements List → choose "Headings" tab
        → Hear: the full heading outline of the page
        → This tells you every major section available
```

After these three steps, you know:

- **What** page you are on (step 1)
- **Where** the page regions are (step 2)
- **What** content is available and how it is organized (step 3)

From there, navigate with purpose: `D` to jump to regions, `H` or `3` to jump to content headings, `K` for links, `B` for buttons.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (VoiceOver - macOS) - 10-second orientation sequence</summary>

```text
Step 1: Quick Nav H (with Quick Nav on) or VO+Cmd+H → navigate to h1
        → Hear: what page type are you on? (repo name / "Issues" / issue title / PR title)

Step 2: VO+U → press Left/Right Arrow to choose "Landmarks" → Up/Down to explore
        → Build a map: "Navigation Menu, Repository navigation, Main, Add a comment, Pagination"
        → Escape to dismiss the rotor

Step 3: VO+U → press Left/Right Arrow to choose "Headings"
        → Hear: the full heading outline of the page
        → Up/Down to navigate headings; Enter to jump to one
```

After these three steps, you know:

- **What** page you are on (step 1)
- **Where** the page regions are (step 2)
- **What** content is available and how it is organized (step 3)

From there, navigate with purpose: `VO+U → Landmarks` to jump to regions, Quick Nav `H` to jump to content headings, Quick Nav `K` for links, Quick Nav `B` for buttons.

> **VoiceOver tip:** `VO` = `Control+Option`. Turn Quick Nav on/off by pressing `Left Arrow + Right Arrow` simultaneously. Quick Nav lets you use single keys (`H`, `B`, `K`, `T`) without holding `VO`, matching the feel of NVDA/JAWS browse mode.

</details>

## 8. GitHub's Heading Hierarchy in Practice

GitHub uses a predictable heading structure. Learning this pattern means you can navigate any page by heading level alone.

### Repository home

```text
H1: owner/repo-name
  H2: About (sidebar section)
  H2: Releases
  H2: (README sections - whatever the author wrote)
```

### Issues list

```text
H1: Issues
  (no H2s - issues are listed as links, not headings)
  (use I for list items, or 3 for issue headings in some views)
```

### Issue detail

```text
H1: Issue title
  H2: Description
  H2: Activity
    H3: Each comment header (author + timestamp)
```

### Pull request detail - Conversation tab

```text
H1: PR title
  H2: (description, if any)
  H2: Activity
    H3: Each comment header
    H3: Each review submission
    H4: Each inline comment within a review
```

### Pull request detail - Files Changed tab

```text
H1: PR title
  H2: File tree (with "New Files Changed Experience" enabled)
    H3: Each file name heading
      H4: Each diff hunk heading
```

> **Why this matters:** Pressing `3` on a PR Files Changed tab jumps between file headings - this is how you quickly navigate to a specific file without tabbing through the entire diff.

### Learning Cards: GitHub's Heading Hierarchy

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Press `1` for H1 (page identity), `2` for H2 (major sections), `3` for H3 (individual items like comments, files, or issues)
- On the PR Files Changed tab, `3` jumps between file headings and `4` jumps between diff hunks within each file
- Open the heading list (`NVDA+F7` or `Insert+F3`) and use it as a table of contents to jump directly to any section

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- H1 headings on GitHub are displayed in large bold text near the top center of the page; H2 headings use slightly smaller bold text with a horizontal rule above them
- Issue comments (H3) each have a header bar with the author's avatar, name, and timestamp; zoom in on this bar to orient yourself in long discussions
- On the Files Changed tab, each file heading (H3) shows the file path in monospace text with a green/red summary of lines added/removed

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- GitHub's heading hierarchy maps to visual size: H1 is the page title, H2 are section dividers, H3 are individual items within sections
- In the Issues list, issue titles function as H3 headings; scan visually or use `3` to jump between them
- On PR conversations, review comments appear in indented boxes; each box header corresponds to an H3 or H4 heading

</details>

## 9. How GitHub's Layout Changes by Viewport

GitHub is a responsive web application. The layout shifts at different screen widths, and this affects what landmarks and headings you encounter.

### At full desktop width (1200px+)

- File tree and sidebar are visible alongside the main content
- The full repository tab bar is visible
- All landmark regions described above are present

### At tablet width (768-1199px)

- Sidebar may collapse or move below the main content
- Some navigation items may move into a "More" dropdown
- Landmark structure remains the same - only visual position changes

### At mobile width (below 768px)

- Global navigation collapses to a hamburger-style menu
- Tabs may scroll horizontally or collapse
- The landmark structure is the same but the "Navigation Menu" landmark becomes a toggle

**Consistent experience recommendation:** Use your browser maximized or at full desktop width during this workshop. GitHub's landmark and heading structure is most consistent at desktop width. If you hear different landmarks or headings than described in this guide, maximize your browser window.

## 10. The Mental Model - Building Your Internal Map

After your first day of using GitHub, you will have an internal map. Here is what that map should look like:

```text
GitHub as a building:

LOBBY (global nav bar)
  Always here, same on every floor
  Contains: search, your inbox, your identity
  Landmark: "Navigation Menu"

FLOOR SELECTOR (repository nav tabs)
  Changes based on which repo you're in
  Contains: Code, Issues, PRs, Actions, Settings
  Landmark: "Repository navigation"

MAIN ROOM (the primary content area)
  Changes completely depending on which floor you're on
  Landmark: "Main"

MAILBOX (Add a comment)
  At the bottom of Issues and PR Conversation pages
  Landmark: "Add a comment"

ELEVATOR BUTTONS (keyboard shortcuts)
  G+I = Issues floor
  G+P = Pull requests floor
  G+C = Code floor
  G+A = Actions floor
  ? = Show all buttons in this building
```

When you get disoriented:

1. Press `1` - hear the H1 - know what floor you are on
2. Press `D` - hear the landmarks - know what rooms are available
3. Press `NVDA+F7` - see the full outline - know what's in the room

You are never lost. You always have these three fallbacks.

### Learning Cards: Building Your Internal Map

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Memorize the elevator shortcuts: `G I` (Issues), `G P` (Pull Requests), `G C` (Code), `G A` (Actions); press `?` on any page to see the full list
- The "Add a comment" landmark is always at the bottom of Issue and PR Conversation pages; press `D` repeatedly until you hear it to jump directly to the reply box
- If a page feels unfamiliar, fall back to the three-step sequence: `1`, `D`, `NVDA+F7` and you will re-orient within seconds

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Think of GitHub like a building: the top bar (lobby) never changes, the tabs below it (floor selector) change per repo, and the main area (room) changes per page
- When disoriented at high zoom, press `Home` to return to the top of the page where the navigation bar and repo tabs are always visible
- The comment box ("mailbox") at the bottom of issue and PR pages has a distinct white input area with a green "Comment" button on its right

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The mental map is: top bar (always there), repo tabs (one row below), then main content; every GitHub page follows this three-layer stack
- Press `?` on any page to see a popup listing all keyboard shortcuts available on that specific page
- The comment box at the bottom of issues and PRs has a tabbed interface (Write/Preview) and a green Submit button; it is always the last section on the page

</details>

## Try It: The 60-Second Orientation

**Time:** 1 minute | **What you need:** A browser with your screen reader running

Open any GitHub repository - try [github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents](https://github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents) - and prove to yourself that the mental model works:

1. Press `1` - your screen reader announces the repo name. You know where you are.
2. Press `D` - you hear the first landmark. Press `D` again to hear the next one. You now know the rooms on this floor.
3. Press `2` - you jump to the first section heading. Press `2` again to scan the page structure.
4. Press `H` three times - you're moving through headings at any level. You're reading the outline.

**You're done.** Four keys, under a minute. You just navigated a GitHub repository by ear.

> **What success feels like:** You heard a repo name, at least two landmarks, and several headings. If you did, you can orient yourself on *any* GitHub page using these same four keys.

## If You Get Stuck

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| Screen reader says nothing when pressing `1` | Ensure browse mode is active (NVDA: press `Escape`; JAWS: press `Num Pad Plus`). GitHub pages must fully load before heading navigation works. |
| Landmarks announce differently than expected | GitHub updates its landmark structure periodically. Press `D` to cycle landmarks and listen to what is announced rather than expecting exact names. |
| Page seems empty or broken | Some GitHub features require JavaScript. Ensure your browser has JavaScript enabled and try refreshing with `Ctrl+Shift+R`. |
| Cannot find the repository navigation tabs | Press `D` until you hear "Repository navigation" then press `K` or `Tab` to find Code, Issues, Pull Requests tabs. |
| Everything else | Post a comment on your challenge issue describing what you see and hear. A facilitator or buddy can walk you through it. |
| I finished but I am not sure I did it right | Compare your work against the [Challenge 1 reference solution](solutions/solution-01-scavenger-hunt.md). Your version does not need to match exactly -- if you explored the tabs and found the key files, you succeeded. |

currentFacts: The Accessibility Agents collection grows over time. Refer to it as a living catalog rather than asserting a fixed count of agents.
Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.
Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.
Hosts are Alex (warm expert) and Jamie (curious co-host who asks the questions learners hesitate to ask). They are colleagues, not teacher and student.
voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
